newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian inflation falls, best yet to come.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian inflation falls, best yet to come.

text.p: Australia's inflation rate fell to a two year low in the September quarter, with the key underlying rate back within the central bank's target band for the first time in over a year, and analysts see further gains on the way.
"Today's inflation figure was good and the best is yet to come," Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen said.

The consumer price index (CPI), or headline inflation, rose 0.3 percent in the September quarter, and the annual rate fell to 2.1 percent from 3.1 percent at the end of June, slightly below median expectations of a 2.2 percent.
It was the lowest annual CPI since the September quarter 1994, and well below the 5.1 percent peak reached at the end of last year, and the rate seems set to fall further.

"Inflation is improving and the near term outlook is positive," Commonwealth Bank economists said. "Our present projections show headline inflation dipping to an annual rate of around 1.5 percent in the December quarter."

The key underlying rate rate rose 0.5 percent in the quarter, and was 2.4 percent higher over the past 12 months, compared to a 3.1 percent rise in the year to June. The market had expected an underlying rate of 2.5 percent.
It was the first time since the June 1995 quarter that the underlying rate has been under three percent.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) aims to keep underlying inflation, which removes volatile and seasonal items from the CPI, to an average of two to three percent over a run of years.
"A mixture of structural change and flat demand is producing the best inflation numbers in decades," Colonial's Kunnen said.
"We expect underlying inflation to remain below three percent for at least the next 18 months," he said.
The government was also pleased with the slightly better than expected inflation figures.

"This is a good result for the consumer price index for the September quarter ... that's a very good outcome for the Australian economy. What it shows is that we are in a low inflationary growth environment," Treasurer Peter Costello told reporters after the inflation data was released.
But while economists, and politicians welcomed the data, the markets reaction was more subdued.
"It was probably the least reaction I can remember to a CPI number, the high/low today is a five point range on the 10-year bonds," Bain and Company senior economist Ivan Colhoun said.
The Australian dollar was also fairly steady on the data, trading at US$0.7943/48 two hours after the data was released, from a pre-data level of US$0.7937/42.
The reason for the subued reaction was that the market had been expecting the good inflation results, but on their own they were not seen as enough to justify an interest rate cut.
More important to the interest rate and inflation outlook are Thursday's third quarter wages data and beyond that, enterprise bargaining agreements data due in November, economists said.
"Today's result confirms there is room for an interest rate cut," Societe Generale economists said.
"Whether or not the Reserve Bank decides to make one depends to a large extent on Thursday's average weekly earnings result for the September quarter," they said.

Economists surveyed by Reuters expect wages to show a 1.0 percent rise in the three months to August, to be 3.7 percent higher over the year, a level that would be supportive of arguments for a rate cut, economists said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
